tips.title: Induced magnetism only ever pulls
tips.body:
A permanent magnet can attract **or** repel. An induced magnet — a paperclip, a steel nail, anything magnetic that has been brought near a magnet — can only ever **attract**.

So if a question describes two objects *repelling*, both of them must be permanent magnets. That single sentence answers a whole family of exam questions.

tips.title: Field lines leave north
tips.body:
Outside the magnet, every field line runs **from north to south**. "**N**orth is where they are **N**ot going in."

Inside the magnet they run the other way, south to north, which completes the loop — but AQA only asks about the pattern outside.

tips.title: Only four metals are magnetic
tips.body: The spec names **iron, steel, cobalt and nickel**. Aluminium, copper and brass are not magnetic, however metallic they look, and a question that offers you one of those is testing exactly that.

tips.title: Close lines mean a strong field
tips.body:
Field strength shows in the **spacing** of the lines, not their length. They are closest together at the **poles**, which is where the field is strongest, and spread out as you move away.

A drawing with evenly spaced lines has lost the mark for showing how the strength changes.

tips.title: A compass is a tiny bar magnet
tips.body: Whenever a question mentions a compass, replace it in your head with a small bar magnet free to turn. Its north end swings until it points along the field it is sitting in — which is the whole answer to "how do you plot a field?" and to "why does a compass work at all?"

why.matters:
Magnetism is the one force in this course you can feel acting through thin air, and it is the link between electricity and movement. Every motor, loudspeaker, generator and transformer in the next topic rests on the ideas here: what a field is, which way it points, and what it does to a magnetic material placed in it.

It is also the reason a compass has worked for a thousand years, and the best evidence anyone has that the centre of the Earth is molten iron — a place no one has ever been or ever will.

examples.title: Why a fridge door shuts
examples.body:
A fridge magnet is a **permanent** magnet. The steel door is not a magnet at all until the magnet comes near it: the door becomes an **induced** magnet, and induced magnetism is always attraction. That is why the magnet sticks whichever way round you turn it.

Turn two fridge magnets to face each other and the story changes. Now both are permanent, so one way round they pull together and the other way they push apart — the test that tells you whether something is a magnet or merely magnetic.

visual.alt: Two bar magnets side by side, the left one showing its north pole and the right one its south pole, with arrows showing each magnet pulled towards the other

examples.title: The compass, and the centre of the Earth
examples.body:
A magnetic compass is a small bar magnet on a pivot. Left alone it lines up with the field it is in, and outdoors that is the **Earth's** field, so the needle settles pointing roughly north.

That is more interesting than it sounds. A field has to come from somewhere, and the only thing that could produce one on that scale is the Earth's **core**. So a needle costing a pound is the evidence that thousands of kilometres down there is something magnetic — moving molten iron. You cannot dig there; the compass tells you anyway.

steps.title: Poles, and the force between them
steps.body:
Every magnet has two **poles**, a **north** and a **south**. They are the places where **the magnetic forces are strongest**.

Bring two magnets close and they push or pull on each other, without touching:

- **Two like poles repel.** North and north, or south and south.
- **Two unlike poles attract.** North and south.

That push or pull happens across a gap, so it is a **non-contact force** — the same family as gravity and the electrostatic force, and the spec names it as an example of one.

The force is **equal on both magnets**, however different their sizes. A tiny magnet near a large one pulls on the large one exactly as hard as it is pulled.

steps.title: Permanent and induced magnets
steps.body:
This is the distinction most marks in this topic hang on.

**A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field.** It is magnetic whether or not anything else is nearby — a bar magnet, a fridge magnet, a compass needle.

**An induced magnet is a material that becomes a magnet when it is placed in a magnetic field.** A steel paperclip is not a magnet sitting in a drawer. Bring a magnet near and the paperclip becomes one, which is why it can then pick up a second paperclip.

Two consequences the exam asks for again and again:

- **Induced magnetism always causes a force of attraction.** Never repulsion. A permanent magnet can do either.
- **When removed from the magnetic field an induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism quickly.**

> Two objects that **repel** must both be **permanent** magnets, because induced magnetism cannot push.

visuals.alt: A table comparing permanent and induced magnets: a permanent magnet always makes its own field, can attract and repel, and is unchanged when taken away; an induced magnet is magnetic only while in a field, can only attract, and loses most or all of its magnetism quickly when removed

steps.title: What a magnetic field is
steps.body:
**The region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material is called the magnetic field.**

The magnetic materials are worth learning as a list, because a question will offer you a metal that is not on it: **iron, steel, cobalt and nickel**. Aluminium, copper and brass are not magnetic.

Two facts about the force, and they are different facts:

- Between a magnet and **another magnet**, the force can be attraction or repulsion, depending on the poles.
- Between a magnet and a **magnetic material**, the force is **always one of attraction**. The material is being induced, and induced magnetism only pulls.

**The strength of the field depends on the distance from the magnet**, and **the field is strongest at the poles**.

steps.title: Field lines, and which way they point
steps.body:
A field has a direction at every point, and we draw it with **field lines**.

**The direction of the magnetic field at any point is the direction of the force that would act on another north pole placed at that point.** That is the definition, and it is worth learning as a sentence, because it is what fixes the arrows.

It gives the rule you actually use:

> **The direction of a magnetic field line is from the north pole of the magnet to the south pole.**

So, outside the magnet, arrows point **away from north** and **into south**.

Strength shows in the **spacing**:

- Lines **closest together at the poles**, because that is where the field is strongest.
- Lines spreading apart as you move away, because the field weakens with distance.

A drawing with lines the same distance apart everywhere says the field is the same strength everywhere, which is wrong, and drops the mark.

steps.title: Worked example: which bar is the magnet?
steps.body:
Two identical steel bars. One is a permanent magnet, the other is plain steel. You have nothing else. Which is which?

The trap is to bring the two ends together and watch them attract. That happens either way round, and tells you nothing.

visuals.problem: You are given two identical steel bars. One is a permanent magnet and the other is not. Using only the two bars, work out which is the magnet.

steps.text: Bring an end of bar A near an end of bar B. They attract.
steps.note: This rules nothing out. A magnet attracts plain steel by inducing magnetism in it, and it would also attract the unlike pole of a second magnet.

steps.text: Now bring an **end** of bar A to the **middle** of bar B.
steps.note: The middle of a magnet is its neutral region: the poles are at the ends, and that is where the field is strongest.

steps.text: If they attract strongly, **A is the magnet**.
steps.note: A's end is a pole, so it induces magnetism in the steel of B wherever it is held, middle included.

steps.text: If there is little or no attraction, **B is the magnet**.
steps.note: Then A is plain steel with no field of its own, and B's middle is the weakest part of B's field, so there is almost nothing to pull with.

steps.text: Repulsion at any point would settle it at once: only a permanent magnet can repel.
steps.note: With one magnet and one plain bar you will never see it, which is itself the point.

check.prompt: Why is it not enough to bring the two ends together and watch them attract?
check.solution: A magnet attracts plain steel by **inducing** magnetism in it, so attraction happens whichever bar is the magnet.

options: Steel bars are too heavy for any force between them to be noticed

steps.title: Plotting a field with a compass
steps.body:
**A magnetic compass contains a small bar magnet**, free to turn. Put it in a field and its north end swings until it points **along** the field — which makes it an instrument for finding the field's direction anywhere.

That is the method the spec asks you to describe:

1. Put the bar magnet on a sheet of paper and **draw round it**.
2. Place the compass near one pole. Mark a dot at each **end of the needle**.
3. Move the compass so its **tail sits on the dot the head just made**, and mark the new head.
4. Repeat, working across the paper, until you reach the other pole.
5. **Join the dots** into a smooth curve, and put an **arrow** on it in the direction the compass north end pointed.
6. **Start again** from a different point near the pole to build up the whole pattern.

The details that earn marks are the ones people leave out: joining the dots **smoothly**, putting **arrows** on the lines, and repeating from several starting points so the pattern is a pattern rather than one line.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**1.** A magnet is brought near a steel paperclip and picks it up. The paperclip then picks up a second paperclip. Name the kind of magnetism in the first paperclip, and say what happens to it when the magnet is taken away.

**2.** Two bar magnets are placed end to end and push apart. What can you say about the two poles facing each other?

**3.** On a diagram of a bar magnet, a student draws six field lines, all the same distance apart, with no arrows. Give **two** things wrong with the diagram.

**4.** Explain why a compass needle in a room still settles pointing roughly north even with no magnet anywhere near it.

**Answers.** 1. **Induced** magnetism; it loses **most or all** of it **quickly** when the magnet is removed. 2. They are **like** poles — both north, or both south — because like poles repel. 3. The lines should be **closest together at the poles** to show the field is strongest there, and each line needs an **arrow**, pointing from north to south. 4. It is sitting in the **Earth's** magnetic field, and a compass is a small bar magnet that lines up with whatever field it is in.

steps.title: Going deeper: what the compass proves about the Earth
steps.body:
The spec asks you to **explain how the behaviour of a magnetic compass is related to evidence that the core of the Earth must be magnetic**. That is an *explain* question, and it wants a chain, not a fact.

The chain:

1. A compass is a **small bar magnet**, free to turn.
2. It **settles**, and stays settled, so a **force** is acting on it — something is turning it.
3. A force on a magnet means it is sitting in a **magnetic field**.
4. The needle points the same way **everywhere on Earth**, and nothing above ground is near enough or large enough to do that.
5. So the field must belong to the **Earth itself**, and be produced **inside** it — in the **core**.

The usual lost mark is stopping at step 3: *there is a magnetic field*, without saying why the field has to come from inside the planet rather than from something nearby.

**A caution about names.** The end of the needle that points north is called the **north-seeking** pole. Since unlike poles attract, the thing it is being pulled towards must behave as a **magnetic south** pole. So the Earth's magnetic pole up in the Arctic is, magnetically, a south pole. AQA will not ask you to untangle that, but it explains why the spec writes “north(seeking)” rather than just “north”.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- A magnet's **poles** are where the **magnetic forces are strongest**.
- **Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.** Both are **non-contact** forces.
- A **permanent** magnet **produces its own magnetic field**.
- An **induced** magnet **becomes a magnet when placed in a magnetic field**, and **always** causes a force of **attraction**.
- Removed from the field, an induced magnet **loses most or all of its magnetism quickly**.
- Two things that **repel** are therefore both **permanent** magnets.
- The **magnetic field** is the region where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material.
- The magnetic materials are **iron, steel, cobalt and nickel**.
- Between a magnet and a magnetic material the force is **always attraction**.
- Field **strength** depends on **distance**, and is **greatest at the poles**.
- A field line's direction is the direction of the force on a **north pole** placed there, so lines run **north to south** outside the magnet.
- **Closer lines mean a stronger field**; even spacing is a lost mark.
- A **compass contains a small bar magnet** and lines up with the field it is in.
- To **plot** a field: draw round the magnet, dot both ends of the needle, move the tail on to the last dot, repeat, join smoothly, add arrows, start again elsewhere.
- A compass settling the same way everywhere is the **evidence that the Earth's core is magnetic**.

questions.prompt: A bar magnet is placed on a sheet of paper. Describe how to use a plotting compass to find the shape of its magnetic field, and explain how the finished diagram should show that the field is strongest at the poles.
questions.solution:
Put the bar magnet on the paper and draw round it, so the pattern is recorded against a known position. Place the plotting compass near one pole and mark a dot at each end of the needle. Move the compass so that its tail sits on the dot the head has just made, and mark the new head; repeat this across the paper until you reach the other pole. Join the dots into a smooth curve and put an arrow on it, pointing the way the compass north end pointed, which is from the north pole of the magnet to the south pole. Then start again from a different point near the pole, and repeat, until there are enough lines to show the pattern.

The finished diagram shows the strength of the field by the spacing of the lines rather than by their length. They should be drawn closest together at the two poles, because that is where the field is strongest, and spreading further apart with distance from the magnet, because the strength of the field depends on the distance from it.

questions.prompt: A student finds that a magnet picks up a steel paperclip, and that the paperclip then picks up a second paperclip. When the magnet is removed, both paperclips fall. Explain these observations, and explain what the student would have to observe instead to prove that a paperclip was a permanent magnet.
questions.solution:
The magnet is a permanent magnet: it produces its own magnetic field whether or not anything else is near it. When the first paperclip is brought into that field it becomes an induced magnet, and because induced magnetism always causes a force of attraction, it is pulled towards the magnet and picked up. The first paperclip now has a field of its own, so it induces magnetism in the second paperclip in the same way, and that one is attracted and held too.

When the magnet is removed, both paperclips are no longer in a magnetic field. An induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism quickly once it is removed from the field, so neither paperclip stays magnetic and both fall.

To show that a paperclip was a permanent magnet, attraction would not be enough: an induced magnet attracts as well, so attraction tells you only that the object is magnetic. The student would have to bring a known magnet near and observe repulsion. Induced magnetism can never repel, so a repulsion could only come from a permanent magnet.

examTechnique.body:
Say which kind of magnet you mean. “Magnet” on its own earns little; “permanent magnet” and “induced magnet” are the words the mark scheme is looking for.

If two things repel, say that both must be permanent magnets, and say why: induced magnetism can only attract.

For a field diagram, draw the lines all the way from one pole to the other, put an arrow on every line pointing from north to south, and draw them closest together at the poles. Even spacing loses the strength mark.

Quoting the definition of field direction — the direction of the force on a north pole placed at that point — is worth doing when a question asks why the arrows point the way they do.

When describing how to plot a field, include the three steps people forget: move the compass so it follows on from the last dot, join the dots smoothly, and repeat from several starting points.

For the Earth’s core, give the chain rather than the fact. A compass settles, so a force acts, so there is a field; it acts everywhere on Earth and nothing above ground explains it, so the source is inside the planet.
examinerErrors: Saying an induced magnet can repel. It never can — induced magnetism always causes attraction.
Calling a paperclip or a steel nail a magnet without saying it is an *induced* one.
Drawing field lines evenly spaced, which says the field is the same strength everywhere.
Leaving the arrows off field lines, or pointing them from south to north outside the magnet.
Drawing field lines that stop in mid-air instead of running from one pole to the other.
Offering aluminium, copper or brass as a magnetic material. The four are iron, steel, cobalt and nickel.
Saying a compass points north “because of the North Pole” without mentioning the Earth’s magnetic field.
Stopping the Earth’s-core answer at “there is a magnetic field” without saying why its source must be inside the planet.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer never says “magnetic” where it could say “permanent magnet” or “induced magnet”, and reaches for repulsion as the test that separates them: attraction shows only that something is magnetic, while repulsion can come only from a permanent magnet. It explains an induced magnet in two steps — placed in a field, it becomes a magnet; taken out of it, it loses most or all of that quickly — rather than asserting the result. On a field diagram it gets three things right at once: lines running pole to pole, arrows from north to south on every one, and spacing that tightens at the poles because that is where the field is strongest. Asked about the Earth, it gives the chain from a settling needle to a force, to a field, to a field that acts everywhere, to a source inside the planet, and it is careful to say that this is evidence about the core rather than a direct observation of it.
